instrument.full_name: Declaration Renouncing the Use, in Time of War, of Explosive Projectiles Under 400 Grammes Weight
instrument.adopted_at: Saint Petersburg (text settled by the International Military Commission, then signed by the representatives of the participating governments)
instrument.depositary: None designated. The Declaration contains no depositary clause, and the place where the signed original is kept was not established in the sources reviewed.
instrument.key_non_parties: The ICRC treaty database lists 19 participants, all of which signed or acceded in 1868 or 1869; it records no later accession. Among the states then in existence, Spain did not attend the Commission (Keefer 2014), and the United States did not take part: the Russian memorandum read at the first session records its reply to the first circular as still awaited (Martens, NRG, vol. 18, no. 115). Neither appears in the ICRC list. The ICRC customary IHL study states that Estonia adhered in 1991; the ICRC treaty database does not list Estonia, and no instrument of accession was found.
instrument.duration_clause: No term is stated. The renunciation is stated without limit of time (operative para. 1); its application in a given war depends on the general participation clause (operative paras. 3 and 4).
instrument.withdrawal_clause: The Declaration contains no withdrawal or denunciation clause. Operative para. 4 provides only that the engagement ceases to be compulsory in a particular war once a non-contracting or non-acceding party joins one of the belligerents.
instrument.amendment_clause: No amendment procedure is stated. Operative para. 5 records that the contracting or acceding parties reserve the right to come to a further understanding whenever a precise proposition is drawn up in view of future improvements in armament. At the second session the Russian Foreign Ministry delegate explained that this wording made any further understanding optional rather than obligatory (Protocol No. 2, Martens, NRG, vol. 18, no. 115).
instrument.entry_into_force_requirements: The text contains no ratification or entry-into-force clause. The ICRC records entry into force on 11 December 1868, the date of signature, and gives each signatory a ratification/accession date of 11 December 1868. Accession is open to states that did not send delegates to the Commission (operative para. 2); the text does not say when an accession takes effect. At the first session the representatives of Bavaria and Württemberg said they could act only subject to ratification by their governments (Protocol No. 1); whether any ratification followed was not established.
instrument.count_basis: The Declaration has no articles. Citations use: preamble, para. 1 (introductory paragraph); preambular considering clauses 1 to 5; operative paras. 1 to 5; and the closing formula. Word count: authentic French text as reproduced by the ICRC (French page), from the introductory paragraph to the dating formula, excluding the title, the heading inserted mid-text on the ICRC page and the signature line, counted with whitespace tokenization (elided forms such as d'examiner count as one word): 372. The ICRC English translation counted on the same basis (local PDF) gives 384 words. The French wording was checked against the 1873 printing in Martens, Nouveau recueil général, vol. 18, no. 116.
instrument.weapons_systems_limited: Projectiles weighing less than 400 grammes that are explosive or charged with fulminating or inflammable substances, as used by land or naval forces. In 1868 this meant explosive and incendiary rifle and small-calibre bullets; artillery shells, being heavier, were not covered.
instrument.key_provisions: The contracting parties renounce, in case of war among themselves, the employment by their military or naval troops of any projectile weighing less than 400 grammes that is explosive or charged with fulminating or inflammable substances (operative para. 1). They will invite states that did not send delegates to the Commission to accede (operative para. 2). The engagement binds only contracting or acceding parties in a war between two or more of them and does not apply towards non-parties (operative para. 3); it ceases to be compulsory once a non-party joins one of the belligerents (operative para. 4). The parties reserve the right to reach a further understanding on future improvements in armament (operative para. 5). The preamble states that the only legitimate object of war is to weaken the military forces of the enemy and that arms which uselessly aggravate the sufferings of disabled men or render their death inevitable are contrary to the laws of humanity.
instrument.behavior_change: Partly. Russia had issued explosive rifle bullets to its army from 1863, and several other states had developed similar ammunition (ICRC introduction; Keefer 2014); the Declaration renounced their wartime use against other parties. It did not restrict production, possession or testing: at the second session the Commission replaced the word "armement" with "emploi" on the proposal of the Russian War Minister so as not to forbid peacetime trials (Protocol No. 2). Kalshoven (2016) judges that the introduction of rifle shells was effectively forestalled.
instrument.historical_background: Russia introduced an explosive rifle bullet in 1863 for use against ammunition wagons and in 1867 a version that exploded on contact with soft targets (ICRC introduction). Unwilling to use it against troops or to let others gain an advantage from it, the Russian government proposed an international ban by circular of 9 (21) May 1868, followed by a draft protocol on 17 (29) June and a third circular on 5 (17) July after Prussia asked for a broader inquiry. An International Military Commission chaired by War Minister Dmitry Milutin met in three sessions between 28 October (9 November) and 4 (16) November 1868, fixed the 400-gramme limit, extended the ban to incendiary projectiles and, at British request, added a general participation clause. The Declaration was signed on 29 November (11 December) 1868 (Martens, NRG, vol. 18, nos. 115 and 116).

related.missing: International Military Commission (St Petersburg, 28 October/9 November to 4/16 November 1868)

provisions.provision: Renounce use of explosive, fulminating or inflammable projectiles under 400 grammes
provisions.unit: grammes (projectile weight below which use is renounced)
provisions.bound_parties_detail: Every contracting or acceding party, on identical terms ("engage mutually")
provisions.geographic_scope: No geographic limit; applies to use by military or naval troops in a war between two or more contracting or acceding parties
provisions.exceptions: Binding only in a war between contracting or acceding parties and not towards non-parties (operative para. 3); ceases to be compulsory once a non-contracting or non-acceding party joins a belligerent (operative para. 4). Covers use in war only; peacetime trials were deliberately left outside the text (Protocol No. 2). The ICRC customary IHL study (Rule 78) reports that later practice modified the rule, so that exploding anti-aircraft and anti-materiel bullets are used without objection and only anti-personnel use of bullets that explode within the human body is treated as prohibited; Article 18 of the 1923 Hague Rules of Air Warfare (never adopted as a treaty) stated that tracer, incendiary or explosive projectiles by or against aircraft are not forbidden.
provisions.text_or_paraphrase: The Contracting Parties engage mutually to renounce, in case of war among themselves, the employment by their military or naval troops of any projectile of a weight below 400 grammes, which is either explosive or charged with fulminating or inflammable substances.
provisions.locator: Operative para. 1 (French: "Les parties contractantes s'engagent à renoncer mutuellement ...")

provisions.bound_parties_detail: The contracting parties collectively; the text names no state or body to issue the invitations
provisions.text_or_paraphrase: The parties will invite all states that did not take part in the deliberations of the International Military Commission by sending delegates to accede to the engagement. Coded Other because it is a procedural undertaking, not a restriction on a weapon activity.

events.event: First Russian circular proposes a ban
events.attribution: Russian memorandum read at the first session, printed in Martens, NRG, vol. 18, no. 115; also Keefer (2014)
events.description: The Russian government asked other governments whether the wartime use of explosive bullets should be abolished by international agreement, declaring itself ready to adopt the rule for its own army if all others did. According to the memorandum, every government except the United States, whose reply was awaited, accepted the principle.
events.locator: Nouveau recueil général, vol. 18 (1873), no. 115, Russian memorandum annexed to Protocol No. 1

events.event: Second circular circulates a draft protocol
events.attribution: Russian memorandum, printed in Martens, NRG, vol. 18, no. 115
events.description: Gorchakov circulated a draft protocol renouncing explosive projectiles for rifles, mitrailleuses and grapeshot, with a reserved further understanding on future improvements in armament, and asked governments to empower their representatives in St Petersburg to negotiate and sign it.

events.event: Prussia proposes a broader inquiry
events.attribution: Keefer (2014), citing the Prussian communication of 10 July 1868 in The National Archives, FO 83/316
events.description: According to Keefer, Prussia asked that the inquiry be widened, on the model of the 1856 Declaration of Paris, into a general rule on weapons causing excessive harm.
events.locator: War in History 21(4), p. 452 and n. 28
events.date_as_reported: 10 July 1868, as given by Keefer, who states that he uses Western (Gregorian) dates

events.event: Third circular convenes a military commission
events.attribution: Russian memorandum, printed in Martens, NRG, vol. 18, no. 115
events.description: Following the Prussian note, Gorchakov issued a third circular. The memorandum records that Turkey, Bavaria, Portugal, Belgium, the Netherlands and Switzerland accepted the Prussian proposal but did not intend to send special military agents.

events.event: First session of the International Military Commission
events.actors: Representatives of 16 governments; War Minister Dmitry Milutin presiding
events.attribution: Protocol No. 1, printed in Martens, NRG, vol. 18, no. 115
events.description: Milutin opened the Commission. Delegates stated their instructions; France and Britain would discuss only the ban on explosive bullets, and Prussia, having no precise proposal, accepted that its suggested wider exchange be set aside. The Commission agreed on a complete exclusion of explosive projectiles below a weight to be fixed, the 400-gramme figure being referred to governments.

events.event: Second session settles weight, incendiaries and reciprocity
events.actors: Commission members; Persia attended from this session
events.attribution: Protocol No. 2, printed in Martens, NRG, vol. 18, no. 115
events.description: The Commission retained the 400-gramme limit (Sweden and Norway found it too high but did not oppose it), extended the ban to projectiles charged with fulminating or inflammable substances, replaced "armament" with "employment" so as not to forbid peacetime trials, added "land or naval" troops, and at the request of the British commissioner adopted the clauses limiting the engagement to wars between parties and ending it when a non-party joins a belligerent.

events.event: Commission approves the wording and closes
events.attribution: Protocol No. 3, printed in Martens, NRG, vol. 18, no. 115
events.description: Turkey reported its government's acceptance of the 400-gramme limit. The Commission adopted the final wording and left it to the Foreign Ministry and the plenipotentiaries to give the declaration its international form.

events.event: Declaration signed at St Petersburg
events.actors: Austria-Hungary, Bavaria, Belgium, Denmark, France, Great Britain, Greece, Italy, Netherlands, Persia, Portugal, Prussia and the North German Confederation, Russia, Sweden and Norway, Switzerland, Turkey, Württemberg
events.attribution: Text and signatures, Martens, NRG, vol. 18, no. 116; ICRC IHL treaty database
events.description: Representatives of 17 governments signed the Declaration, dated 29 November (11 December) 1868.

events.event: Entry into force
events.attribution: ICRC IHL treaty database
events.description: The ICRC records entry into force on the date of signature; the text itself contains no entry-into-force clause.

events.event: Baden accedes
events.attribution: ICRC IHL treaty database (states parties)
events.description: The ICRC lists Baden's accession on 11 January 1869. Baden had told Russia in 1868 that it was ready to sign any protocol agreed among the great powers (Russian memorandum, NRG, vol. 18, no. 115).

events.event: Brazil accedes
events.attribution: ICRC IHL treaty database (states parties)
events.description: The ICRC lists Brazil's accession on 23 October 1869. Keefer (2014) reports the British ambassador's despatch of 28 October 1869 on Brazil's adherence.

events.event: Violation claims in the Franco-Prussian War
events.actors: Not identified in the source consulted (France and the North German Confederation were the belligerents)
events.attribution: Reported by Keefer (2014)
events.description: Keefer states that claims of violations were made during the Franco-Prussian War. He gives no details of who made them or of any response, and no formal finding was identified in the sources reviewed.

events.event: Prohibition repeated in the Brussels Declaration
events.attribution: ICRC customary IHL study, Rule 78; date from Keefer (2014)
events.description: The ICRC study states that the St Petersburg prohibition was repeated in Article 13(e) of the Brussels Declaration, which never entered into force; Kalshoven (2016) quotes the Russian invitation describing the conference as a step towards developing the Geneva Convention of 1864 and the Declaration of St Petersburg.

events.event: Violation claims in the Anglo-Transvaal war
events.actors: Not identified in the source consulted
events.attribution: Reported by Keefer (2014)
events.description: Keefer states that claims of violations were also made during the "Boer War of 1880-1". He gives no details. The South African Republic does not appear in the ICRC list of parties, so under operative para. 3 the Declaration would not have applied between the belligerents; no formal finding was identified in the sources reviewed.

events.event: Hague Declarations cite St Petersburg in their preambles
events.actors: Powers represented at the First Hague Peace Conference
events.attribution: Texts of Hague Declarations IV,1, IV,2 and IV,3 (ICRC IHL treaty database)
events.description: The three 1899 Hague Declarations on balloons, asphyxiating gases and expanding bullets each state that their signatories were inspired by the sentiments which found expression in the Declaration of St Petersburg. Keefer reports that delegations first considered adding the new bans as a protocol to the 1868 Declaration but concluded them as separate, independent instruments.
events.locator: Preamble of each declaration; Keefer, p. 462

events.event: Hague Rules of Air Warfare permit explosive projectiles against aircraft
events.attribution: Text of the 1923 Hague Rules (ICRC IHL database); ICRC customary IHL study, Rule 78; Kalshoven (2016)
events.description: Article 18 of the draft rules states that tracer, incendiary or explosive projectiles by or against aircraft are not forbidden, for parties and non-parties to the St Petersburg Declaration alike. The rules were never adopted as a treaty. The ICRC study treats Article 18 as reflecting a change in practice that began in the First World War; Kalshoven describes it as customary law setting aside the treaty rule.

events.event: ICRC expert meeting on 12.7 mm exploding bullets
events.actors: ICRC; governmental experts from four states that manufactured or stocked the ammunition
events.attribution: ICRC customary IHL study, Rule 78 and practice
events.description: After tests showed that certain 12.7 mm bullets exploded in human tissue simulant, the ICRC convened experts from four states, participating in their personal capacity, who agreed that targeting combatants with bullets whose foreseeable effect was to explode on impact with the human body would be contrary to the object and purpose of the Declaration.

events.event: ICRC report to the CCW Preparatory Committee
events.attribution: Cited in the ICRC customary IHL study, Rule 78, n. 8
events.description: The ICRC submitted a report, "Ensuring respect for the 1868 St Petersburg Declaration: Prohibiting the use of certain explosive projectiles", to the Third Preparatory Committee for the Second Review Conference of the CCW. The report itself was not retrieved.
events.date_as_reported: 2001 (the Second CCW Review Conference was held in 2001; the report's exact date was not verified)

events.event: ICRC customary IHL study published
events.attribution: ICRC customary IHL study, Rule 78; publication year from the ICRC President's statement of 24 November 2008
events.description: Rule 78 of the study states that the anti-personnel use of bullets which explode within the human body is prohibited as customary law in international and non-international armed conflicts, and that practice since 1868 has modified the treaty prohibition.

events.event: 140th anniversary conference in St Petersburg
events.actors: ICRC; Inter-Parliamentary Assembly of the CIS; Russian government
events.attribution: Statement by ICRC President Jakob Kellenberger (ICRC, archived copy)
events.description: The ICRC and the CIS Inter-Parliamentary Assembly held an international conference on the 140th anniversary of the Declaration. A transcript attached to the Notion record shows Prime Minister Vladimir Putin addressing the conference, describing Russia's role in drafting the Declaration and proposing that states review new armaments for compliance with humanitarian law.

events.event: 150th anniversary conference in St Petersburg
events.attribution: Address by ICRC President Peter Maurer (ICRC)
events.description: At an international conference marking the 150th anniversary, the ICRC President described the Declaration as the first formal multilateral agreement to prohibit the use of a weapon in war and as pre-emptive, banning the weapon before it had been used.

overview_md: The St Petersburg Declaration of 29 November (11 December) 1868 is the first formal agreement prohibiting the use of a particular weapon in war ([ICRC](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/ihl-treaties/st-petersburg-decl-1868)). Seventeen governments whose representatives had met in an International Military Commission convened by Russia signed it, and Baden and Brazil acceded in 1869. The parties renounce, in wars among themselves, the use by their land or naval forces of any projectile weighing less than 400 grammes that is explosive or charged with fulminating or inflammable substances, a rule aimed at explosive and incendiary rifle bullets. The engagement binds only parties in wars between parties and lapses if a non-party joins a belligerent. The ICRC lists it as in force, although its customary IHL study reports that later practice narrowed the rule to the anti-personnel use of bullets that explode within the human body. Its preamble, which states that the only legitimate object of war is to weaken the military forces of the enemy, is widely cited as an early statement of the prohibition of unnecessary suffering.
provisions_md:
The Declaration has no numbered articles. Citations refer to the introductory paragraph, the five preambular considering clauses and the five operative paragraphs of the [authentic French text](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/fr/ihl-treaties/st-petersburg-decl-1868/declaration), checked against the [1873 printing in Martens, Nouveau recueil général, vol. 18, no. 116](https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_K4oBAAAAYAAJ). The ICRC [English translation](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/ihl-treaties/st-petersburg-decl-1868/declaration) follows the same order.

### Preamble
- The Commission is said to have fixed by common agreement "the technical limits at which the necessities of war ought to yield to the requirements of humanity" (preamble, para. 1).
- The considering clauses state that the only legitimate object of war is to weaken the military forces of the enemy, that disabling the greatest possible number of men suffices, and that arms which uselessly aggravate the sufferings of disabled men or render their death inevitable are contrary to the laws of humanity (considering clauses 1 to 5).

### The prohibition
- The contracting parties renounce, in case of war among themselves, the employment by their military or naval troops of any projectile weighing less than 400 grammes that is explosive or charged with fulminating or inflammable substances (operative para. 1).
- The rule restricts use in war only. The Commission chose the word "employment" rather than "armament" so as not to forbid peacetime trials ([Protocol No. 2](https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_K4oBAAAAYAAJ)). Artillery shells, heavier than 400 grammes, are outside it.

### Bound parties and the general participation clause
- The engagement binds contracting and acceding parties identically, but only in a war between two or more of them, and does not apply towards non-parties (operative para. 3).
- It ceases to be compulsory once a non-contracting or non-acceding party joins one of the belligerents (operative para. 4). The British commissioner asked for this wording at the second session ([Protocol No. 2](https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_K4oBAAAAYAAJ)).

### Accession and future developments
- The parties will invite states that did not send delegates to the Commission to accede (operative para. 2).
- The parties reserve the right to reach a further understanding whenever a precise proposition is made about future improvements in armament, in order to maintain the principles they have established (operative para. 5). The Russian Foreign Ministry delegate told the Commission that this left any further understanding optional ([Protocol No. 2](https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_K4oBAAAAYAAJ)).
- The text contains no provisions on information, verification, consultation, dispute settlement or enforcement.

### Later interpretation
The text has not been amended. The ICRC customary IHL study ([Rule 78](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/customary-ihl/v1/rule78)) reports that exploding anti-aircraft bullets were introduced in the First World War and lighter grenades and exploding anti-materiel bullets later, without objection, so that state practice now treats only the anti-personnel use of bullets that explode within the human body as prohibited. Article 18 of the [1923 Hague Rules of Air Warfare](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/ihl-treaties/hague-rules-1923), never adopted as a treaty, stated that explosive projectiles by or against aircraft are not forbidden.
participation_md:
- **Signature.** Representatives of 17 governments signed at St Petersburg on 29 November (11 December) 1868 ([Martens, NRG, vol. 18, no. 116](https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_K4oBAAAAYAAJ)). The text provides no signature period and no ratification clause.
- **Entry into force.** No entry-into-force clause. The [ICRC](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/ihl-treaties/st-petersburg-decl-1868) gives 11 December 1868 and records each signatory's ratification/accession on that date. At the first session the Bavarian and Württemberg representatives spoke of acting subject to ratification; whether any ratification followed was not established.
- **Accession.** Open to states that did not send delegates to the Commission (operative para. 2). The ICRC lists Baden (11 January 1869) and Brazil (23 October 1869) and no later accession. The ICRC customary IHL study states that Estonia adhered in 1991, but the ICRC treaty database does not list Estonia and no instrument was found.
- **Participants.** 19 as listed by the ICRC (checked 11 October 2026), including seven historical entities that the ICRC lists without successors (Austria-Hungary, Baden, Bavaria, Persia, Prussia and the North German Confederation, Sweden and Norway, and Württemberg). The ICRC lists the Ottoman and Russian participations under Türkiye and the Russian Federation; this record reports those listings and does not code successions.
- **Application.** Only in a war between parties; the engagement lapses if a non-party joins a belligerent (operative paras. 3 and 4).
- **Duration and withdrawal.** No term and no withdrawal or denunciation clause.
- **Amendment and review.** No amendment procedure and no review conferences; operative para. 5 reserves an optional further understanding on new weapons.
- **Depositary.** None designated; the custody of the signed original was not established.
history_md:
### Origins
Russia introduced an explosive rifle bullet in 1863, intended for blowing up ammunition wagons, and in 1867 a version that exploded on contact with soft targets ([ICRC introduction](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/ihl-treaties/st-petersburg-decl-1868)). Keefer reports that Prussia, Austria, Switzerland and Bavaria also developed such bullets ([Keefer 2014](https://doi.org/10.1177/0968344513505810)). By circular of 9 (21) May 1868 Russia proposed an international ban; a draft protocol followed on 17 (29) June and, after Prussia asked for a broader inquiry, a third circular on 5 (17) July convened a military commission ([Russian memorandum, NRG, vol. 18, no. 115](https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_K4oBAAAAYAAJ)).

### The International Military Commission
Chaired by War Minister Dmitry Milutin, the Commission met on 28 October (9 November), 1 (13) November and 4 (16) November 1868 ([Protocols Nos. 1 to 3](https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_K4oBAAAAYAAJ)). It set aside the Prussian idea of a general rule, adopted the 400-gramme limit separating banned projectiles from artillery shells, extended the ban to incendiary projectiles and, at British request, added the general participation clause. Keefer argues that Britain insisted on reciprocity to keep such weapons available against non-European adversaries and reports that London authorized signature only after confirming the Declaration would not apply to Central Asia ([Keefer 2014](https://doi.org/10.1177/0968344513505810)). Spain and the United States did not take part. The Declaration was signed on 29 November (11 December) 1868, and Baden and Brazil acceded in 1869 ([ICRC states parties](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/ihl-treaties/st-petersburg-decl-1868/state-parties)).

### Compliance
Keefer reports that claims of violations were made during the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 to 1871 and the Anglo-Transvaal war of 1880 to 1881 (allegations; no details given, and no formal finding was identified in the sources reviewed) ([Keefer 2014](https://doi.org/10.1177/0968344513505810)).

### Later influence
The ICRC study states the prohibition was repeated in the 1874 Brussels Declaration ([Rule 78](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/customary-ihl/v1/rule78)). The three 1899 Hague Declarations, including the [Declaration on expanding bullets](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/ihl-treaties/hague-decl-iv-3-1899), cite in their preambles the sentiments of the St Petersburg Declaration; Keefer reports that delegates first considered a protocol to the 1868 Declaration before choosing separate instruments. Article 18 of the [1923 Hague Rules of Air Warfare](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/ihl-treaties/hague-rules-1923) allowed explosive projectiles against aircraft. In 1999 ICRC-convened experts agreed that targeting combatants with 12.7 mm bullets foreseeably exploding in the body would be contrary to the Declaration's object and purpose, and the 2005 customary IHL study (Rule 78) treats the anti-personnel use of such bullets as prohibited ([Rule 78](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/customary-ihl/v1/rule78)). The ICRC marked the 140th and 150th anniversaries at conferences in St Petersburg in [2008](http://web.archive.org/web/20090701123820/http://www.icrc.org:80/web/eng/siteeng0.nsf/html/st-petersburg-declaration-281108) and [2018](https://www.icrc.org/en/document/icrc-president-address-150th-anniversary-st-petersburg-declaration).

coding_notes.note: Coded Declaration, the parties' own title. The form label does not imply a political instrument: the text states that the contracting parties "engage mutually" and the ICRC describes the Declaration as having the force of law.
Legally binding, from the text (an engagement that is "compulsory" for contracting or acceding parties, operative paras. 1 and 3) and the ICRC's characterization.

Date Adopted records formal adoption of the text: here 11 December 1868 (Gregorian), the signature that concluded the Declaration, given in the document as 29 November (11 December) 1868 because Russia used the Julian calendar. The International Military Commission had approved the wording earlier, at its third session on 4 (16) November 1868; that preparatory approval is recorded as an event, not as adoption.
The Declaration was signed by 17 governments on a single day; there was no signature period. Other states could only accede (operative para. 2).
11 December 1868, as recorded by the ICRC. The text contains no entry-into-force or ratification clause.

No current-party count is coded. The ICRC lists 19 participants: 17 original signatories and two accessions in 1869 (Baden and Brazil), list checked 11 October 2026; the ICRC customary IHL study likewise describes nineteen states adhering in 1868-69. Several rows leave present-day participation unresolved, so the historical count is not a count of current states parties. Estonia, reported in the customary IHL study, is not listed.
17 signatures printed under the text in Martens, NRG, vol. 18, no. 116, matching the ICRC signature list. The Commission itself had 16 delegations at its first session; Persia joined at the second.
Multilateral (open): operative para. 2 invites all states that did not send delegates to the Commission to accede.

Land and Sea, from the text's reference to "military or naval troops" ("troupes de terre ou de mer"), added at Belgium's proposal at the second session. Air warfare did not exist in 1868; later treatment of aircraft is described in prose.

The rule is defined by projectile weight and effect, not by launcher. Small arms & light weapons reflects its target, explosive bullets for rifles and mitrailleuses (the Commission president said artillery was excluded, Protocol No. 1); Incendiary weapons reflects the words "fulminating or inflammable substances", added to cover incendiary bullets (Protocol No. 2).

None. Operative para. 5 reserves an optional future understanding on new armaments but creates no mechanism; the Russian Foreign Ministry delegate described it as facultative (Protocol No. 2). Coded from the instrument's own text.
Not specified in text: no declarations, data or reports are required. Coded from the instrument's own text.
Not specified in text. The general participation clause (operative paras. 3 and 4) limits when the rule applies but provides no consequence for non-compliance. Coded from the instrument's own text.
Not specified in text. Coded from the instrument's own text.
Not specified in text. Coded from the instrument's own text.
Not specified in text. Coded from the instrument's own text.

Not specified in text. The text assigns no function to a non-party. Operative para. 2 provides for inviting states that were not at the Commission to accede; that is eligibility to become a party, recorded under participation structure, not a third-party role. Coded from the instrument's own text.
Not Specified: the text does not address reservations. Coded from the instrument's own text.
Indefinite: no term is stated. Coded from the instrument's own text.

None stated: there is no withdrawal or denunciation clause. The lapse of the engagement when a non-party joins a war (operative para. 4) is a condition of application, not withdrawal. Coded from the instrument's own text.
None stated. Operative para. 5 contemplates further agreements on new weapons, not amendment of this text. Coded from the instrument's own text.

In force, as recorded by the ICRC. The ICRC customary IHL study reports that later practice modified the prohibition (exploding anti-aircraft and anti-materiel bullets), and Kalshoven considers that customary law set aside the treaty rule for aircraft; these are described as later interpretation, not termination.

Reproduction: the texts used are the ICRC's reproduction (French and English translation, from Schindler and Toman) and the 1873 printing in Martens, Nouveau recueil général. No depositary or government treaty-series text was consulted.

produced_by points to the International Military Commission, which has no row. No relation to the 1899 Hague Declaration (IV,3) is coded: it is a separate instrument that cites this Declaration's sentiments in its preamble, not a protocol to, amendment of or replacement for it, and the parties did not negotiate the two together. The link is described in the history section.

The renunciation is one row because its explosive, fulminating and inflammable limbs bind identically; both weapon families are tagged. The general participation clause and the reserved future understanding are not separate obligations on a weapon activity and appear in exceptions and prose.
